blocks.content: Introduction to Voltage drop & resistance clues
Interpret low voltage/dim load symptoms and resistance-related faults.

items.definition: An unstable or fluctuating milliohmmeter reading on a bonding strap indicates a poor, intermittent contact — almost always caused by corrosion or contamination at one or both attachment points. Correct action: inspect, clean, and re-measure.
items.analogy: Like a loose headphone plug causing crackling audio — the connection exists but isn't solid.

items.definition: If voltage at a load is lower than expected, excessive resistance upstream is consuming voltage (V=IR voltage drop). Causes: corroded connections, undersized wire, loose terminals. The extra resistance steals voltage from the load.
items.analogy: Water pressure drops at the end of a garden hose with a partially kinked section — the kink steals the pressure before it reaches the nozzle.

items.definition: A voltage drop between source and load is caused by resistance in the wiring path: V_drop = I × R_wire. Common sources: corroded connectors, undersized wire, loose terminals, bad splices. Even small resistance creates measurable drops at normal aircraft current levels.
items.analogy: Friction in a pipe reduces water pressure at the outlet — more friction (resistance) means more pressure (voltage) lost before the water (current) arrives.

items.definition: Dim bulbs in a lighting circuit indicate reduced voltage at the bulb — caused by excessive resistance upstream stealing voltage (V=IR drop). Common causes: corroded connectors, loose terminals, undersized wire, or a poor ground return.
items.analogy: Like a clogged showerhead producing weak pressure — the water supply is fine, but something in the path is choking the flow.

items.definition: A 0.5V drop can occur anywhere in the complete circuit loop: supply wiring, connectors, AND the ground return path. Don't forget that the ground wire and ground connections also have resistance. A bad ground creates the same voltage drop symptom as a bad supply wire.
items.analogy: A water system with a constricted intake pipe AND a constricted drain — both limit overall flow and pressure.

blocks.question: During a bonding check, the milliohmmeter reading fluctuates rather than settling on a stable value. What does this indicate and what should be done?
choices: The strap is good — fluctuation is normal for milliohmmeter readings
The meter is faulty — replace the instrument
There is an intermittent contact — inspect and clean attachment points for corrosion
The circuit has AC interference — use DC excitation mode
blocks.feedback: A fluctuating reading means the contact is intermittent — not consistently solid. This is characteristic of corrosion or contamination at the bonding surface. Inspect and clean both attachment points before re-measuring.

blocks.question: A nav radio shows 24V supply at the bus but only 21V at the radio connector. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Excessive resistance in the wiring or connectors between the bus and radio
There is an open circuit between the bus and the radio
The radio is drawing more current than rated
The voltage regulator output is too low
blocks.feedback: The 3V drop is a classic sign of excessive resistance in the wiring path (V=IR). Corroded pins, a loose terminal, or undersized wire creates resistance that drops voltage before it reaches the load. An open would give 0V at the radio.

blocks.question: You measure 24V at the bus and 23.5V at a downstream connector. What does this 0.5V difference most likely indicate?
choices: A blown fuse between the bus and connector
Normal voltage variation within tolerance
Resistance in the wiring or connectors between those two points
The downstream equipment is drawing excessive current
blocks.feedback: V_drop = I × R_path. A measurable voltage difference between source and load means there is resistance in the path consuming voltage. This points to corroded connectors, a bad terminal, undersized wire, or a poor splice.

blocks.question: Navigation lights in an aircraft are noticeably dimmer than when the aircraft was new. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The bulbs are drawing more current as they age
There is an open circuit in one of the branches
Excessive resistance from corroded connections or undersized wiring is causing a voltage drop
The bus voltage has increased beyond normal limits
blocks.feedback: Dim but functioning lights indicate reduced voltage — not zero volts. Corroded connectors, loose pins, or undersized wire create resistance that drops voltage before it reaches the bulbs. This is the classic presentation of a wiring/connection problem.

blocks.question: A 0.5V drop is measured between the bus and a downstream load in a 24V circuit. Which of the following should be inspected as potential causes?
choices: The wiring, connectors, and ground return path between the source and the load
Only the ground connection at the load
Only the positive supply wire
The load itself — it must be drawing too much current
blocks.feedback: Voltage drop can occur in any part of the circuit: supply wire, connectors, and the ground return. All three must be checked. Focusing only on one side misses the complete picture — a degraded ground is just as capable of creating a measured drop.
